claim: Snell et al., 2024 (abstract): compute-optimal allocation of test-time compute by difficulty improves its efficiency 'by more than 4x compared to a best-of-N baseline' on MATH with a PaLM 2-S* base model; in the PRM-search setting it 'nearly' outperforms best-of-N with 4x less compute 'at points', and the difficulty bins come from an oracle check or from predicted difficulty whose cost is left out.
Snell et al., 2024: on the most challenging questions 'we observe very little benefits from scaling up test-time compute' (MATH).

Snell et al., 2024: choosing the search strategy by difficulty bin nearly matched PRM best-of-N with up to 4x less test-time compute (16 against 64 generations) at low budgets on MATH with PaLM 2-S*; this held with oracle bins and also with model-predicted bins, whose cost (a learned verifier averaged over 2,048 samples per question) the analysis leaves out; at higher budgets the gain shrinks with predicted bins.
note: Narrowed after refute A49. The collect file's 'up to 4x' stands for low budgets; the abstract says 'more than 4x'.

claim: Snell et al., 2024: the difficulty bins assume 'oracle access to a ground-truth correctness checking function, which is of course not available upon deployment'.
note: The refute A49 adds that predicted difficulty (a learned verifier over 2,048 samples per question, cost not accounted for) is the other source of bins, not only the oracle.

claim: Han et al., 2024: on average over six maths sets with GPT-4o-mini, TALE-EP, a token budget the model first estimates itself and puts in the prompt, gives 'a 67% reduction in token usage while maintaining accuracy with less than a 3% decrease' against vanilla chain-of-thought; the accuracy loss grew with difficulty, 8 points on MathBench-College (78 to 70).
note: Narrowed after refute A50: the under 3 percent is an average across the sets (Table 3).

claim: Han et al., 2024: TALE-EP cut output tokens 67 % on average (461 to 149 tokens in Table 3) and expense 59 % against vanilla CoT on six maths sets (GSM8K, GSM8K-Zero, four MathBench sets) with GPT-4o-mini; the text states 80.22 % average accuracy.
note: Narrowed after refute A50. The Table 3 average row reads 81.03 %, not the 80.22 % of the text (paper.txt 493).

claim: Han et al., 2024: averaged over the six sets (Table 3), TALE-EP scored 81.03 % against 83.75 % for vanilla CoT, a visible accuracy loss.
note: Corrected: the collect file's 'on one set' is wrong; 83.75 and 81.03 are the Average row of Table 3 (raw.txt 443-447, 627). Refute A50.

claim: Han et al., 2024: an observed 'token elasticity' means a token budget that is too small makes the output cost rise again (paper.txt 303-306).
Han et al., 2024: TALE rests on an 'implicit monotonicity assumption' that a budget which works stays working when raised, which 'may not strictly hold in every instance' (raw.txt 167).

Muennighoff et al., 2025 (s1): budget forcing, which extends thinking by suppressing the end-of-thinking token and appending 'Wait', lifts s1-32B 'from 50% to 57% on AIME24' (30 questions; Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct tuned on 1,000 examples).

Muennighoff et al., 2025 (s1): the AIME24 gain from budget forcing 'eventually flattens out at six times' (six suppressions of the end of thinking, not a multiple of tokens), and suppressing the delimiter too often 'can lead the model into repetitive loops' (raw.txt 395).
Muennighoff et al., 2025 (s1): 'for 12 out of the 30 evaluation questions the model generates a response that exceeds the context window', leading to a large performance drop (raw.txt 733).

Aggarwal et al., 2024 (AutoMix): sending a query to the larger model only when a POMDP router, fed by the small model's few-shot self-check, judges the answer unreliable gives 'reducing computational cost by over 50% for comparable performance' across five context-grounded datasets, two with long documents; cost is a fixed per-query unit ratio, not tokens (raw.txt 7, 332, 333).
Aggarwal et al., 2024 (AutoMix): AutoMix-POMDP is 'the only method that yields positive gains across all configurations', best on DIPLOMAT, 'averaging 122% across all models' (raw.txt 467).
note: The quote names no metric; the collect file (line 61) says the score is IBC.

claim: Aggarwal et al., 2024 (AutoMix): the cost model fixes a relative cost of 1 unit for the small model and 60, 100 or 200 units for GPT-4 per query ('we model fixed costs', raw.txt 224, 332); the cost is a price ratio, not a count of tokens.
Liu et al., 2025 (BATS): given a larger tool-call budget, agents 'lack budget awareness and quickly hit a performance ceiling' (raw.txt 5).

Liu et al., 2025 (BATS): on BrowseComp with Gemini-2.5-Pro, a Budget Tracker with a budget of 10 tool calls reached comparable accuracy to ReAct at 100 (12.8 against 12.6 percent), using 40.4% fewer search calls and reducing the unified cost, which counts tool use plus priced tokens, by 31.3% (raw.txt 124, 187, 1041).
note: Narrowed after refute A52: the 31.3 percent is a unified cost, not tokens alone.

claim: Liu et al., 2025 (BATS): under 100 tool uses, BATS obtained 24.6% on BrowseComp using Gemini-2.5-Pro (raw.txt 370).
Liu et al., 2025 (BATS): the budget is set in tool calls because 'pre-determining an accurate token budget for multi-step agentic tasks is often impractical' (raw.txt 65).
Liu et al., 2026 (INTENT): with explicit cost feedback in the prompt, 'it still violates budgets in a substantial fraction of tasks', 32.8% for GPT 4.1 mini (raw.txt 339).
Liu et al., 2026 (INTENT): the method 'strictly enforces hard budget feasibility' (raw.txt 9, abstract).
Fang et al., 2026 (ITBC): 'the method yields positive aggregate gains over four audited baselines under the same hard dual-budget protocol' (raw.txt 5).
note: The collect file gives no headline number; the gains are not numerically verified (line 97). The collect file cites raw.txt 3; the sentence is at raw.txt 5.
